Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 21, verse 78–79:

And Dawud and Sulayman... ﴿and We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ (21:78)

What was the story of the field about which Prophet Dawud (Dawud) and Prophet Sulayman (Sulayman), peace be upon them both, gave judgment? Narrators say that two men came to Prophet Dawud. One was the owner of a field, that is, of crops and a vineyard, and the other owned sheep. The owner of the field said that the sheep of this man spread into his field at night, ate everything, and nothing was left in the field. Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) gave the verdict that the man should take the sheep of the other man in exchange for the vineyard. The owner of the sheep went to Prophet Sulayman (peace be upon him), related the matter before him, and told him that Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) had given this judgment. Prophet Sulayman (peace be upon him) went to his father and said: "O Prophet of Allah, the judgment is not what you have decided." He said: "How so?" He said: "Hand over the sheep to the owner of the field or the vineyard so that he may benefit from them, and give the field to the owner of the sheep so that he may work on it, and when it is restored to the condition it was in, return each to its owner, so that each person gives to the other what is in his possession: the owner of the field takes back his field and the owner of the sheep takes back his sheep." Then Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) said: "The correct judgment is the one you have made." And he enforced Sulayman's (peace be upon him) judgment.

It should be remembered that Prophet Dawud and Prophet Sulayman, peace be upon them both, gave their judgments as judges through ijtihad (independent reasoning). Allah was also watching their judgment. Allah inspired Prophet Sulayman (peace be upon him) with a more suitable and firmer judgment, and the way Sulayman understood it was better.

Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) considered only the payment of compensation for the loss. This was pure justice. But Prophet Sulayman (peace be upon him), along with justice, also considered construction and development, and as a result of justice he put both parties to work on construction and development. This second form of justice is more constructive, beneficial and positive, and it is the grace and inspiration of Allah that He gives to whomever He wills.

Both Prophet Dawud and Prophet Sulayman, peace be upon them both, had authority of judgment, knowledge and the power to decide.

﴿And to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ (12:97 as cited in the text) — "We gave judgment and knowledge to both of them." Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) made no error in his judgment, but Prophet Sulayman's (peace be upon him) judgment was better because it resulted from inspiration.

After this, the Qur'an mentions the particular matters that were given separately to Prophet Dawud and Prophet Sulayman, peace be upon them both, first to Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him).

﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] along with Dawud, and the birds [as well]; and We were doers [of that]. And We taught him the making of armor for you to protect you from your violence. So are you grateful?﴾ (21:79–80, as cited in the text)

The psalms of Prophet Dawud are well known. This was the praise of Allah which he recited with a beautiful voice. The atmosphere would be filled with the echo of his voice, and the mountains and birds would repeat it along with him.

When the heart of a servant becomes connected to his Lord, he feels as though he has become united with this entire universe, that the heart of the whole universe beats along with his, and all the barriers and veils that create distances between the various kinds and species of Allah's creatures, due to the awareness of duality, are removed. When a person reaches this station, the consciences of all these kinds merge with the conscience of this universe.

In some moments a light appears such that the soul feels that it is one with this universe. Everything has come within it, and at such moments the soul does not feel that there is anything outside of it. Nor does it feel that it is separate from its surroundings. The entire environment becomes lost in the human soul, and the human being becomes lost in his environment.

From the Qur'anic text we understand that when Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) recited praise with a beautiful voice, he forgot the self present in his distinct, detailed and particular station. His soul would enter into that divine shade which overshadows this universe. Upon this entire universe, whether it is inanimate creation or living, Prophet Dawud would feel that this whole universe was reciting praise along with him, and just as he was praising, so was it. Then it would seem that the entire universe, in the form of a chorus, like a group, was singing the praise, glorification, and declaration of Allah's oneness.

﴿And there is not a thing except that it exalts [Allah] by His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ (17:44). Only the person whose veils are removed, whose distances dissolve, and who moves along with the universe and the souls of the cosmos, all of which face towards Allah, understands this glorification.

﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] along with Dawud, and the birds; and We were doers [of that]﴾ (21:79). What is difficult for Allah? Or can anything defy the command of Allah when He wills it, whether it happens among people or not?

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 21, verse 78–79:

And Dawud and Sulayman... ﴿and We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ (21:78)

What was the story of the field about which Prophet Dawud (Dawud) and Prophet Sulayman (Sulayman), peace be upon them both, gave judgment? Narrators say that two men came to Prophet Dawud. One was the owner of a field, that is, of crops and a vineyard, and the other owned sheep. The owner of the field said that the sheep of this man spread into his field at night, ate everything, and nothing was left in the field. Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) gave the verdict that the man should take the sheep of the other man in exchange for the vineyard. The owner of the sheep went to Prophet Sulayman (peace be upon him), related the matter before him, and told him that Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) had given this judgment. Prophet Sulayman (peace be upon him) went to his father and said: "O Prophet of Allah, the judgment is not what you have decided." He said: "How so?" He said: "Hand over the sheep to the owner of the field or the vineyard so that he may benefit from them, and give the field to the owner of the sheep so that he may work on it, and when it is restored to the condition it was in, return each to its owner, so that each person gives to the other what is in his possession: the owner of the field takes back his field and the owner of the sheep takes back his sheep." Then Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) said: "The correct judgment is the one you have made." And he enforced Sulayman's (peace be upon him) judgment.

It should be remembered that Prophet Dawud and Prophet Sulayman, peace be upon them both, gave their judgments as judges through ijtihad (independent reasoning). Allah was also watching their judgment. Allah inspired Prophet Sulayman (peace be upon him) with a more suitable and firmer judgment, and the way Sulayman understood it was better.

Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) considered only the payment of compensation for the loss. This was pure justice. But Prophet Sulayman (peace be upon him), along with justice, also considered construction and development, and as a result of justice he put both parties to work on construction and development. This second form of justice is more constructive, beneficial and positive, and it is the grace and inspiration of Allah that He gives to whomever He wills.

Both Prophet Dawud and Prophet Sulayman, peace be upon them both, had authority of judgment, knowledge and the power to decide.

﴿And to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ (12:97 as cited in the text) — "We gave judgment and knowledge to both of them." Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) made no error in his judgment, but Prophet Sulayman's (peace be upon him) judgment was better because it resulted from inspiration.

After this, the Qur'an mentions the particular matters that were given separately to Prophet Dawud and Prophet Sulayman, peace be upon them both, first to Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him).

﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] along with Dawud, and the birds [as well]; and We were doers [of that]. And We taught him the making of armor for you to protect you from your violence. So are you grateful?﴾ (21:79–80, as cited in the text)

The psalms of Prophet Dawud are well known. This was the praise of Allah which he recited with a beautiful voice. The atmosphere would be filled with the echo of his voice, and the mountains and birds would repeat it along with him.

When the heart of a servant becomes connected to his Lord, he feels as though he has become united with this entire universe, that the heart of the whole universe beats along with his, and all the barriers and veils that create distances between the various kinds and species of Allah's creatures, due to the awareness of duality, are removed. When a person reaches this station, the consciences of all these kinds merge with the conscience of this universe.

In some moments a light appears such that the soul feels that it is one with this universe. Everything has come within it, and at such moments the soul does not feel that there is anything outside of it. Nor does it feel that it is separate from its surroundings. The entire environment becomes lost in the human soul, and the human being becomes lost in his environment.

From the Qur'anic text we understand that when Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) recited praise with a beautiful voice, he forgot the self present in his distinct, detailed and particular station. His soul would enter into that divine shade which overshadows this universe. Upon this entire universe, whether it is inanimate creation or living, Prophet Dawud would feel that this whole universe was reciting praise along with him, and just as he was praising, so was it. Then it would seem that the entire universe, in the form of a chorus, like a group, was singing the praise, glorification, and declaration of Allah's oneness.

﴿And there is not a thing except that it exalts [Allah] by His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ (17:44). Only the person whose veils are removed, whose distances dissolve, and who moves along with the universe and the souls of the cosmos, all of which face towards Allah, understands this glorification.

﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] along with Dawud, and the birds; and We were doers [of that]﴾ (21:79). What is difficult for Allah? Or can anything defy the command of Allah when He wills it, whether it happens among people or not?

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 21, verse 80:

And We taught him the craft of making armour for you, so that it might protect you from your violence (against one another). Will you then be grateful? (21:80)

This is the craft of armour whose rings pass through one another. Before this, armour was made as a single rigid sheet. Forming armour by inserting rings into one another makes it softer and easier to use. It appears that this advanced form of armour was first invented by Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him), through the teaching of Allah. Allah says that by teaching Dawud (peace be upon him) this skill, He conferred a great favour upon you, since in war you are protected from one another's blows.

"So that it might protect you from your violence against one another" (21:80): that is, in battle. Having mentioned this favour, Allah asks again: "Will you then be grateful?" This question is meant to make people understand and to urge them to gratitude.

Islamic civilisation has progressed step by step. Humanity did not become civilised and advanced all at once in a single leap. The task of worldly progress is connected with the vicegerency of the earth (khilafah ard), and it has been placed upon man. Allah has placed within man the capacity to move forward one step each day and to adapt his life to the progress of each day. It is worth noting that it is contrary to human nature for a person to adapt his entire life to a new system at once, because such a sudden change alters his habits and established ways of working, and giving an entirely new system all at once requires a considerable time for a person to restart his ordinary life from the beginning. Therefore the will of Allah's wisdom is that after every major change in the system of life, people be given suitable time before the next change; sometimes this time is short and sometimes it is a longer period.

The unbearable tension on the nerves of the world today, and the restlessness within people, are largely due to the fact that, because of scientific discoveries and rapid repeated changes in the system of society, humanity is not given the chance to breathe and rest, so that it may enjoy the blessings of the modern system for a period of time. Revolution follows revolution.

That was the matter concerning Dawud (peace be upon him). As for Sulayman (peace be upon him), he too was given many miracles.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 21, verses 81–82:

﴿And to Sulayman We subjected the wind, blowing vigorously, running by his command towards the land which We had blessed. And We had knowledge of all things. And of the devils, We subjected to him those who dived for him and did other work besides that, and We were their keeper.﴾ (21:81–82)

There are many matters, many narrations and many stories famous about Sulayman (peace be upon him). Most of them are either taken from Isra'iliyyat (narratives of Israelite origin) or are the product of illusions and imaginings. But in this desert of narrations we do not want to lose our way. We wish to confine ourselves within the limits of the Qur'an. Apart from the Qur'an, there is no authentic narration about Sulayman (peace be upon him).

The Qur'an mentions only to this extent: the wind was subjected to him, that is, a swift-moving wind. This wind used to blow towards a blessed land. The blessed land refers to the present land of Syria, since there is an allusion to it in the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Now the question is how this wind was subjected to him.

One story concerns a throne of wind or a carpet of wind, on which Sulayman (peace be upon him) and his attendants would sit, rise into the air, and travel towards Syria, and in the blink of an eye they would be in Syria. This journey, it is said, would take a month by camel, and they would return in the same way. This narration is supported by appeal to the verse of Surah Saba in which it is said:

﴿And to Sulayman the wind; its morning course was a month's journey and its evening course was a month's journey.﴾ (34:12)

But the Qur'an nowhere mentions this carpet of wind, and it is not mentioned in any authentic hadith. Therefore we have found no authentic proof for narrations of this kind.

It is better to understand the subjection of the wind to mean that, by Allah's command, this wind used to blow in such a way that it covered a month's distance from one direction in a morning and evening. How this journey was accomplished is a matter of the works of Divine power. We cannot ask how it blew. Allah created the laws of nature, and He can turn these forces of nature in whichever direction He wills. Of the principles of nature in this universe, mankind has so far learned only a few. It is possible that there are some hidden physical laws of Allah of which we are not yet aware, and the manifestation and disclosure of these principles may occur when mankind becomes capable of bearing them and it is Allah's command.

﴿And We had knowledge of all things.﴾ (21:81) Absolute and unrestricted knowledge is in Our possession. As for human knowledge, it is limited.

The same is the case with the subjection of the jinn, who dived for him in sea and land, and extracted treasures of the earth for Sulayman (peace be upon him), or performed other services for him. Jinn refers to a creation that is hidden. From the explicit verses of the Qur'an it is established that there is a creation called jinn, which we cannot see. From among this creation, certain individuals were subjected to Sulayman (peace be upon him), who dived for him and performed other works. Allah placed them under his control so that they could neither flee nor cause corruption. Nor did they obey him by their own will. Allah can exercise full control over His creation and use His creation in whatever manner He wishes.

In Fi Zilal we go as far as this, and this is the limit within which the probability of error is low. Therefore, we have no need to dive into Isra'iliyyat.

Allah tested Dawud and Sulayman (peace be upon them both) through prosperity and through blessings. He tested Dawud (peace be upon him) in judgment. He tested Sulayman (peace be upon them both) concerning horses (details will come in Surah Sad, so we do not raise these discussions here). These discussions are in their own place. Here, mention of the outcome is necessary. Dawud (peace be upon him) was patient, Sulayman (peace be upon them both) was also patient, and after the trials they sought forgiveness and pardon from Allah, and they passed through the test and trial successfully. Thus they were ones who rendered thanks to Allah for His blessings.

﴿And [mention] Ayyub, when he called out to his Lord: "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful."﴾ [21:83] ... ﴿and a reminder for the worshippers.﴾ [21:84]

The story of Hazrat Ayyub (peace be upon him) is one of the most beautiful of the stories of trial in the Holy Qur'an. Wherever this story appears in the Qur'an, it appears in summary form; its details are not given. Here the supplication of Hazrat Ayyub and the acceptance of his supplication are mentioned, because the theme and subject of this surah is mercy upon His servants, good treatment of them, and their support in trials, whether the trial is in the form of denial by their people, as in the stories of Ibrahim, Lut and Nuh (peace be upon them), or a trial through the blessings of Allah, as with Dawud and Sulayman (peace be upon them), or a trial through illness and the like, as in the story of Hazrat Ayyub (peace be upon him).

In the supplication that Hazrat Ayyub made here, he only described his condition and mentioned the attribute of his Lord: ﴿You are the most merciful of the merciful﴾ [12:38 as cited]. After this he did not say, "Change my circumstances." This is because he was patient in the face of calamities; he did not make any proposal or demand before Allah. This was his manner of adab and respect in the presence of the Lord of Honour. Hazrat Ayyub (peace be upon him) was a person of such patience and gratitude that in the hardest of circumstances he would remain patient and would not lament. His patience became so famous that his example is always cited. He was so patient and grateful that he did not even pray for the removal of this affliction; he left the whole matter to Allah, since Allah knew everything, so what need was there to ask?

When Hazrat Ayyub (peace be upon him) turned to his Lord with this confidence and in this respectful manner, Allah immediately accepted his supplication; the trial ended and the mercy of Allah arrived. Not only was his distress removed, but his family was also restored to him, and He gave him as much again besides.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 21, verse 84:

﴿Fastajabna lahu...﴾ ... ﴿mithlahum ma'ahum﴾ (12:48)?

"We answered his prayer and removed the affliction that was upon him, and We gave him not only his family but also others like them along with them."

The illness that had afflicted his body went away, and he immediately became healthy. Allah gave back to him the family he had been deprived of, and gave him others like them. It has been said that sons were given in place of sons, or that sons and grandsons were given.

﴿Rahmatan min 'indina﴾ (12:48): "Every mercy of Allah is His favour. It is a pure favour; otherwise, we do not deserve it."

In relation to trial, the meaning of this is very important: trials keep coming to worshippers, for example, the difficulties of worship, intellectual difficulties, and the demands of faith. This is a most serious matter, not a joke. The Islamic way of life is a great trust, and this trust is given only to those who can bear its burden and fulfil its demands and obligations. It is not merely a matter of saying something with the tongue, nor merely a claim; therefore patience is necessary, so that worshippers may prove true in trial.

After this, the Holy Qur'an only alludes to Hazrat Isma'il, Hazrat Idris and Hazrat Dhul-Kifl.

﴿And Isma'il and Idris and Dhul-Kifl, all of them were among the steadfast. And We admitted them into Our mercy. Indeed, they were among the righteous.﴾ (21:85–86)

In the life circumstances of these prophets, the element of patience holds great importance. Regarding Hazrat Isma'il (peace be upon him), it was commanded that he be slaughtered. When this matter came to his knowledge, he submitted himself, and this was an exemplary model of patience.

﴿O my father, do what you are commanded. You will find me, God willing, among the steadfast.﴾ (37:102)

Regarding Hazrat Idris, it has been mentioned earlier that his time and place are unknown. Some people have given the opinion that he is that Idris, after whose death the Egyptians began to worship him and associated with him many tales and stories, such as that he was the first teacher of mankind, who taught mankind agriculture and taught industry. But there is no definitive proof for this claim. We are certain that he too demonstrated exemplary patience in some trial, which the Holy Qur'an deemed necessary to mention.

Regarding the time and place of Hazrat Dhul-Kifl, there is also no information. The prevailing view is that he was among the prophets of the Children of Israel. Some narrations state that he was among the righteous of the Children of Israel. His achievement was that he took responsibility for the care and service of one of the prophets of the Children of Israel, and he gave him his caliphate on the guarantee of three conditions: that he would worship throughout the night, be fasting every day, and not become angry when passing judgment. He fulfilled these guarantees, therefore he was named Dhul-Kifl. But this too is only one opinion, and there is no proof for it. The Holy Qur'an here only specifies that they were patient.

Now the story of Prophet Yunus (peace be upon him). He is also called Dhul-Nun.

﴿And Dhul-Nun, when he went off in anger...﴾ to ﴿Thus do We deliver the believers﴾ (21:87–88).

The story of Prophet Yunus (peace be upon him) is also presented here as a brief allusion, as is the style of this surah, and its details are in Surah As-Saffat. However, it is necessary that we give some essential details here so that the allusions here are properly understood. He is called the one of the fish (Dhul-Nun) because, when he was thrown from the ship, a fish swallowed him. The story was that he was sent to a village to spread the Islamic call. The people of the village did not heed him, and he became very angry at this. Due to this anger, he left that place in displeasure, and did not exercise patience and perseverance in bearing the difficulties of the Islamic call among them. He thought: "The land of God is not narrow," meaning, God's creation is vast and there are many other villages; if these people do not accept the call, God will turn others toward it. This is the meaning of ﴿So he thought that We would not decree against him﴾ (21:87), that is, "lan naqdira 'alayhi" means "lam nudayyiq 'alayhi" (We did not constrict him). His anger and constricted heart led him to resolve to leave the village. He reached the seashore. There a ship was ready. He boarded it. The ship was surrounded by the waves of the sea. The sailor said that if it were not lightened, everyone would drown. Upon this, they cast lots. The lot fell upon Prophet Yunus. The people threw him into the sea, or he himself jumped in. The fish swallowed him, and he came to a narrower place still. He was then in darkness: one darkness of the belly of the fish, a second darkness of the sea, and a third darkness of the night. He called upon his Lord thus:

﴿There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers﴾ (21:87). God accepted his supplication and delivered him from the distress in which he was. The fish cast him onto the shore. The subsequent events are detailed in Surah As-Saffat. Here, this much was necessary.

In this part of the story of Prophet Yunus (peace be upon him) there are lessons and points for reflection, so a pause here is necessary. Prophet Yunus (peace be upon him) did not show patience in the face of the difficulties in the path of the Islamic call. His heart was overwhelmed; he abandoned the responsibilities of the call and, in anger, set out from that village. When he left, he was in severe distress and anger. God subjected him to difficulties which, compared with the troubles coming from those who denied, were lesser. Had he not repented and not acknowledged his wrong against himself, the Islamic call, and his duties, God would not have delivered him from this calamity. But the Divine Power accepted his repentance, protected him, and freed him from that grief.

Those who carry the Islamic call must bear the duties and difficulties of the call. If people deny, they must be patient with them. If they cause harm, they must be patient. The truth is that for a truthful person, being called a liar has a very bitter effect on the soul. But this is the nature of the responsibilities of prophethood: whether people accept or not, those who carry the Islamic call must develop endurance, be patient, and display steadfastness. It is necessary that they begin the work of the call afresh, start the mission anew and restart the program.

It is their duty not to despair of the work of the call. The spirit of reform can be produced again in hearts, and the work of reforming people can be done, even if a people repeatedly refuse and deny, act arrogantly, and reject the call. If a hundred times of calling does not affect hearts, it may be that the one-hundred-and-first call enters hearts. Sometimes a person succeeds after a thousand and first attempt. If the caller is patient, strives, and does not despair, then after thousands of efforts he may succeed.

The work of the Islamic call is not easy or simple. Stirring people's hearts toward any call is a very difficult task. Winning hearts is harder than bringing milk from a lion. Falsehood, customs, habits and traditions form a layered system that has blocked the work of the call. Moreover, every society wishes to preserve its present organization and institutions. Present habits and ways of life have settled on hearts like rust, so to revive hearts afresh everything must be done; all sensitive centers must be touched by the movement, and with great difficulty one grasps the vein through which the message reaches. Each step requires great patience, great endurance and great struggle; yet sometimes, with only a casual effort, and when the aching vein of human society is seized, a person reaches the goal with great ease, and a revolution appears in society.

This matter can be explained by a common example. You keep turning the tuning dial of a radio receiver but the desired station does not come in. After repeatedly turning it, suddenly the station comes in. Through repeated efforts sometimes the station does not come in, but sometimes, merely by turning the dial carelessly, the station comes in and programs begin to arrive.

The human heart is like the receiver of a radio, and the caller should not despair; he should keep turning the receiver, keep probing hearts. It may be that at some time people's hearts suddenly become ready to accept it, and people begin to look up toward the horizon. It may be that a person's thousand efforts fail, and in the thousand-and-first attempt we attain the desired goal.

It is very easy for a caller to be overcome by anger, to become upset that people do not accept my words. He may abandon the people and sit at ease; fine, his agitation will subside, his nerves will cool. But what will become of the call, and of the Islamic call? Who will return, and who will call the denying and abandoned people?

The real matter is the call. The personality of the caller is not the ultimate aim. If the caller becomes agitated, or his chest is constricted, he should be patient and not leave his path. It is best for his own self that he be patient and not let his heart be constricted by people's words. He should not display impatience, and certainly should not do so because of people's denial and their words.

As for the caller's own self, what is it really? He is merely an instrument in the hand of Divine power. The real work of the call is done by God Himself; He is the protector of the call. The caller should fulfill his duty in all circumstances, find ways to work in every atmosphere, and leave the outcome to God. Guidance is in the hand of God.

The truth is that in the story of Dhul-Nun there is a great lesson for the callers to truth. They must derive this lesson with attention. When Prophet Dhul-Nun (peace be upon him) repented, reviewed his position, and returned to his work, there is a great lesson in this for the workers of the Islamic call. Is it not fitting that the callers to truth reflect upon it? ﴿Thus do We deliver the believers﴾ (21:88), "And thus We deliver the believers."

Prophet Yunus (peace be upon him) did not show patience in the face of the difficulties in the path of the Islamic call. His heart was overwhelmed; he abandoned the responsibilities of the call and, in anger, set out from that village. When he left, he was in severe distress and anger. God subjected him to difficulties which, compared with the troubles coming from those who denied, were lesser. Had he not repented and not acknowledged his wrong against himself, the Islamic call, and his duties, God would not have delivered him from this calamity. But the Divine Power accepted his repentance, protected him, and freed him from that grief.

Those who carry the Islamic call must bear the duties and difficulties of the call. If people deny, they must be patient with them. If they cause harm, they must be patient. The truth is that for a truthful person, being called a liar has a very bitter effect on the soul. But this is the nature of the responsibilities of prophethood: whether people accept or not, those who carry the Islamic call must develop endurance, be patient, and display steadfastness. It is necessary that they begin the work of the call afresh, start the mission anew and restart the program.

It is their duty not to despair of the work of the call. The spirit of reform can be produced again in hearts, and the work of reforming people can be done, even if a people repeatedly refuse and deny, act arrogantly, and reject the call. If a hundred times of calling does not affect hearts, it may be that the one-hundred-and-first call enters hearts. Sometimes a person succeeds after a thousand and first attempt. If the caller is patient, strives, and does not despair, then after thousands of efforts he may succeed.

The work of the Islamic call is not easy or simple. Stirring people's hearts toward any call is a very difficult task. Winning hearts is harder than bringing milk from a lion. Falsehood, customs, habits and traditions form a layered system that has blocked the work of the call. Moreover, every society wishes to preserve its present organization and institutions. Present habits and ways of life have settled on hearts like rust, so to revive hearts afresh everything must be done; all sensitive centers must be touched by the movement, and with great difficulty one grasps the vein through which the message reaches. Each step requires great patience, great endurance and great struggle; yet sometimes, with only a casual effort, and when the aching vein of human society is seized, a person reaches the goal with great ease, and a revolution appears in society.

This matter can be explained by a common example. You keep turning the tuning dial of a radio receiver but the desired station does not come in. After repeatedly turning it, suddenly the station comes in. Through repeated efforts sometimes the station does not come in, but sometimes, merely by turning the dial carelessly, the station comes in and programs begin to arrive.

The human heart is like the receiver of a radio, and the caller should not despair; he should keep turning the receiver, keep probing hearts. It may be that at some time people's hearts suddenly become ready to accept it, and people begin to look up toward the horizon. It may be that a person's thousand efforts fail, and in the thousand-and-first attempt we attain the desired goal.

It is very easy for a caller to be overcome by anger, to become upset that people do not accept my words. He may abandon the people and sit at ease; fine, his agitation will subside, his nerves will cool. But what will become of the call, and of the Islamic call? Who will return, and who will call the denying and abandoned people?

The real matter is the call. The personality of the caller is not the ultimate aim. If the caller becomes agitated, or his chest is constricted, he should be patient and not leave his path. It is best for his own self that he be patient and not let his heart be constricted by people's words. He should not display impatience, and certainly should not do so because of people's denial and their words.

As for the caller's own self, what is it really? He is merely an instrument in the hand of Divine power. The real work of the call is done by God Himself; He is the protector of the call. The caller should fulfill his duty in all circumstances, find ways to work in every atmosphere, and leave the outcome to God. Guidance is in the hand of God.

The truth is that in the story of Dhul-Nun there is a great lesson for the callers to truth. They must derive this lesson with attention. When Prophet Dhul-Nun (peace be upon him) repented, reviewed his position, and returned to his work, there is a great lesson in this for the workers of the Islamic call. Is it not fitting that the callers to truth reflect upon it? Then, in the prayer of Prophet Yunus (peace be upon him), his supplication in the darkness, and its acceptance by God, there is also good news for the callers to truth. Was it not said:

﴿Thus do We deliver the believers﴾ (21:88), "And thus We deliver the believers."

Now, a brief allusion to the story of Prophet Zakariyya and Yahya (peace be upon them both), and the acceptance of Zakariyya's supplication:

﴿And Zakariyya ... humble﴾ (21:90).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 21, verses 89–90:

The story of the birth of Yahya (John) has already passed in Surah Maryam and Surah Ali 'Imran, with great detail. Here, as with the other narratives, there are only hints. It begins with the supplication of Zakariyya (Zechariah):

﴿Lord, do not leave me alone (without an heir)﴾ (21:89). That is, that I should have no heir who would be the guardian of the affairs of the Temple after me. Zakariyya (peace be upon him) was the custodian of the Temple (place of worship) of the Children of Israel. This event occurred before the birth of 'Isa (Jesus) (peace be upon him). Zakariyya (peace be upon him) knew well that the final heir of worship, places of worship, and the wealth of all people is none other than Allah. Therefore he said:

﴿And You are the best of the inheritors﴾ (21:89). But his real intention was that after him, for his family, his religion and his property, he should have a good successor, because in earthly vicegerency it is the human being who carries out the work of the hand of divine power. The acceptance of supplication also comes immediately.

﴿So We answered him and gave him Yahya, and We made his wife fit for him﴾ (21:90). She was barren and not fit for childbearing, but here, as in other narratives, the discourse is abridged within its context and the reader is taken directly to the outcome, that is, the answering of the supplication.

﴿Indeed they used to hasten to good deeds﴾ (21:90). So Allah hastened the acceptance of the supplication.

﴿And they used to call upon Us with hope and fear﴾ (21:90). Hope, so that Allah would be pleased, and fear, that Allah would not be displeased. Their hearts maintained a firm connection with Allah. They were always hopeful of Allah's mercy.

﴿And they were humbly submissive to Us﴾ (21:90). They were neither arrogant nor overbearing towards us. These were the qualities because of which Zakariyya and his wife (peace be upon them) deserved that Allah give them an extraordinary son like Yahya. Thus this was a blessed family, deserving of Allah's mercy and pleasure.

At the very end, with reference to 'Isa (peace be upon him), the mention of his mother Maryam (Mary) also comes, with the same brevity.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 21, verse 91:

والتی …للعلمین (91)

Here the name of Maryam has also been omitted, because in the context of mentioning the prophets, what was truly intended was the mention of her son. Her own mention came within the account of her circumstances, and here only that attribute of hers which relates to her son is repeated.

والتی احصنت فرجھا (21 : 91) "She who guarded her chastity." That is, she protected herself from any kind of intercourse. Ihsan (إحصان), in its legal usage, refers to marriage, because being married is in fact the best means of avoiding immorality and adopting chastity. Here the word is used in its linguistic meaning, that is, protecting oneself from every kind of intercourse, whether lawful or unlawful. This is because the Jews accused Maryam of immorality and implicated her with Yusuf al-Najjar (Yusuf the carpenter), who was a servant of the Temple. The widely circulated Gospels say about this matter that Yusuf al-Najjar had contracted marriage with Maryam, but the rukhsati (formal conveyance to the husband's home) had not yet taken place and he had not approached her.

فنفخنا فیھما من روحنا (21 : 91) "And when she guarded her chastity, We breathed into her of Our spirit." The breathing of the spirit (نفخ روح) here is also general and not restricted to any one thing, as it appears in Surah al-Tahrim. We have already given its details in Surah Maryam. In Fi Zilal al-Quran, our method is to keep our discussion limited to the verses of Allah, so we do not go into details here. We proceed with the verses, following them to the end.

وجعلنھا وابنھا ایۃ للعلمین (21 : 91) "And We made her and her son a sign for all the worlds." This was such a miracle and such a sign that no event like it occurred before, nor will one occur after. In the whole of human history it is a unique example. This event was made unparalleled so that for the reflection of all humanity this single event is sufficient. The Hand of Power acts in accordance with the laws of nature that He has made, yet Allah is not Himself bound by the laws that He has made.

At the conclusion of this account of the messengers, in which examples of the messengers, examples of their trials, and examples of Allah's mercies upon them were given, the Qur'an now states a comprehensive matter as a summary of the discourse.

The verse quoted at the top is ﴿Indeed, this, your community, is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me﴾ (21:92).

Note on the verse: the opening fragment "ان……فاعبدون" is a partial quotation of 21:92, which in full reads: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.﴾

Translation of the commentary:

The group of the prophets is one community and one congregation. Their outlook is also one, and they all have been calling to one and the same system of life. All of them turn toward Allah alone. On earth they are one community, and in the heavens their God is one. Their only emblem is that there is no deity except Allah. Thus, with this surah, this final reflection of the lesson also falls into harmony: that all the Messengers have been calling to the word of Tawhid, and the order of this entire universe bears witness to it as a just witness.

**Lesson No. 143: At a Glance**

This is the final lesson of this surah. The earlier lessons mentioned the cosmic laws of creation operating in this universe, which are signs that its Creator is one. The laws according to which Allah sends the messengers are also one, and they show that the creed of all the messengers was one and the same.

This lesson describes the scenes of the Resurrection and its signs. In this scene, the fate of the polytheists and of the partners they associated with Allah is described, and it is explained that Allah alone is the Controller and Administrator who runs the entire universe.

After this, it is stated that Allah has also established laws and divine patterns (Sunan Ilahiyyah) for granting supreme authority on earth, and that the sending of the Seal of the Prophets (ﷺ) is in reality a mercy of Allah upon this world. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is told to leave them to their own condition and to withdraw from them, so that these people may reach the natural end that Allah has appointed for them. The Prophet (ﷺ) is also told to seek Allah's help against their disbelief, denial and mockery. "Leave them to engage in their play and amusement. The Day of Reckoning is not far away."

﴿And they cut their affair among themselves into pieces...﴾ to ﴿they will not be returned﴾ (95)

The messengers form one group. They are founded upon one ideology, and their community is also one community. The foundation of this community is the Kalima Tayyibah (the good word, i.e., the declaration of faith) and Tawhid (the oneness of Allah). The laws of nature operating throughout this entire universe also bear witness to this. This is the fundamental word to which all the messengers, from beginning to end, have called the people. This is the great foundation of Islam. Yes, the detailed system of life and the system of law established by different messengers have nevertheless differed across different eras. These systems were formed in accordance with the capacity for legal action of each period and the stage of development of its people. In them, the experiences of those nations and their intellectual progress and power of perception were kept in view. Life, the means of living, and the manner in which people relate to one another have all been taken into consideration.

Despite the fact that the messengers were one, their outlook on life and their creed were one, the later generations who followed them broke this one religion, ideology and system into pieces. Each group took a single piece of the religion and separated itself. After this, differences among these groups multiplied, enmity began, hostility grew to such an extent that war and conflict broke out, and people began to kill one another on account of religious beliefs, even though the beliefs were one, because the community itself was one.

They have divided their one religion into pieces in the world, but they do not consider that all of them are moving very quickly towards the Resurrection.

"To Us, all of them shall return" (21:93), because there is no place of return except Allah. It is Allah alone who will call them to account, and He knows who among them is upon the truth and who is upon falsehood.

**Surah 21, verse 93 (as cited in the commentary):**

﴿So whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer, his effort will not be denied, and We are recording it for him.﴾

This is the law of action and its recompense. When righteous deeds (amal-e-salih) are built on the foundation of faith (iman), they will not be rejected and their worth will not be denied. They will already be recorded with Allah, and nothing of them can escape being recorded.

Faith must be the basis of deeds so that both faith and action have value. Without faith, righteous deeds cannot exist. Righteous deeds must be the fruit of faith, and indeed they must be its proof. Faith is the foundation of life, because faith is in truth the real connection between the human being and this universe. It is a connection that binds the universe, and everything within it, to the One Creator. All of this then returns to the law of divine power by which the whole universe operates. Until there is a firm foundation, no structure can be raised upon it. The example of righteous deeds is that of a tall building. If such a tall building is not raised on a strong foundation, it will collapse at any moment.

Furthermore, righteous deeds are always the fruit of faith that resides in the heart, but it must be living faith. What is Islam? It is a dynamic belief. When this dynamic belief settles well in the conscience, it then manifests through the human body in the form of righteous deeds. Indeed, righteous deeds are a ripe fruit of faith. This fruit grows and ripens only when the tree stands on roots that penetrate deep into the earth.

This is why, when the Qur'an speaks of action and recompense, it brings faith and action together. Therefore there is no reward for a faith that is frozen, utterly inert, and bears no fruit at all. Likewise, there is no reward for an action that is cut off from faith.

Sometimes a good deed is seen even without faith, but this is a temporary coincidence, because such an action does not follow a complete plan, nor is it based on any principle or law. It arises at times in accordance with a passing emotion or a temporary desire, and behind it there is no real cause or reason that has any substance within this universe. The firm truth is that righteous deeds should be performed for the pleasure of Allah, the Lord of Majesty. Such deeds alone are constructive. Such deeds alone bring about the perfection and progress that Allah has ordained for the progress of life in this world. Thus righteous deeds are a purposeful movement connected with the purpose of this life. A mere temporary emotion or a merely accidental influence is not their cause; rather, they are purposeful action. Moreover, such action should be in harmony with the law of human nature and the law of creation established by the Creator of the universe, just as the whole universe runs according to the law of nature of the Creator. Complete harmony should exist between the two.

The full recompense for deeds is received in the Hereafter, although a part of it may also be received in this world. As for the settlements that were destroyed in this world, they will be punished for their evil deeds in the Hereafter as well. It is not possible that they will not be raised on the plain of gathering (hashr). Certainly, all these people will be raised on the plain of gathering.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 21, verse 95:

﴿And it is impossible for a town which We have destroyed that its people should return.﴾ (21:95)

Here the mention is of destroyed towns, specifically, because earlier it was said:

﴿Unto Us they all shall return.﴾ (21:93) Sometimes it may occur to the mind that the towns which have been destroyed in this world may have been finished forever, that they will not return, and that their reckoning has ended. Therefore, here the emphasis is repeated: these towns will certainly return and come back on the Day of Resurrection, and their coming back is not forbidden. It is simply not possible that destroyed towns would not come. This manner of expression is somewhat strange. Therefore some exegetes have interpreted that "lā" (not) is here superfluous (zā'id), and the meaning is that when these towns have been annihilated, then they cannot return. Others have interpreted that after this destruction, their turning back to guidance is not possible. I think there is no need at all for either of these interpretations. That interpretation of the Qur'anic text is better which conforms to its apparent grammatical construction, and the context of the discourse also provides an indication for the meaning that we have explained.

After this, one of the scenes of the Day of Resurrection is presented here. This scene is introduced with a sign whose appearance will occur in the time close to the Hour: that is, the breaking forth of Ya'juj and Ma'juj (Gog and Magog).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 21, verses 96–97:

حتی اذا ……فعلین (104)

In the discussion of the story of Dhul-Qarnayn in Surah al-Kahf, we said: "Regarding the opening of Yajuj and Majuj, which is mentioned together with the approach of the Hour, it is possible that the approach of the Hour has already occurred with the emergence of the Tatars. The Tatars came out and, in an instant, spread over the East and the West, and they trampled all the lands and kings, because the Qur'an had already said during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'وَاقْتَرَبَتِ السَّاعَةُ' ('the Hour has drawn near'). Moreover, by the nearness of the Hour, the 'nearness' is not determined, because the reckoning of time is entirely different for humans and for Allah. With Allah, one day equals a thousand years."

Here the scenes of that Day are being described, the Day when it will arrive, and the events within the earth that will precede that Day: Yajuj and Majuj will burst forth from every direction, and then they will descend upon the people from the heights. It is the particular manner of the Qur'an that, by presenting the familiar scenes of the earth, it leads a person toward the scenes of the Hereafter.

In the scene of the Hour presented here, there is an element of surprise. Upon seeing this scene suddenly, people will be stunned, and their eyes will remain fixed wide open.

﴿فَإِذَا هِيَ شَاخِصَةٌ أَبْصَارُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ (21:97) "Suddenly, the eyes of those who disbelieved will remain fixed and staring." This scene will be so sudden that, because of its terror, people will not be able to see anything. Here the Qur'an has placed the word "shakhisa" before "abṣār" so that this scene is firmly impressed upon the mind. Now, leaving aside their circumstances and their condition, the Qur'an conveys their dialogue, so that this scene becomes clear on the screen.

﴿قَالُوا يَا وَيْلَنَا قَدْ كُنَّا فِي غَفْلَةٍ مِنْ هَٰذَا بَلْ كُنَّا ظَالِمِينَ﴾ (21:97) "They will say: 'Woe to us! We were heedless of this; rather, we were wrongdoers.'" This is the cry of one upon whom a calamity comes unexpectedly. A frightening reality is suddenly revealed to him. He becomes terrified; his eyes remain wide open; he sees, yet nothing is visible to him. At last he cries out that he is lost, confesses his sin, and feels remorse, but only after the time has passed.

When confession comes after being seized suddenly, being terrified, and then regaining one's senses, the command of Allah is issued immediately:

﴿إِنَّكُمْ وَمَا تَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ حَصَبُ جَهَنَّمَ أَنْتُمْ لَهَا وَارِدُونَ﴾ (21:98) "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you are going to it as its entrants."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 21 (Al-Anbiya), verses 98–100:

Translation:

"Indeed you and whatever you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; to it you will surely come." Suddenly these people are brought to the field of gathering. They stand at the brink of Hell. With great harshness, the angels seize them and their deities and cast them into Hell. They are thrown there and, becoming fuel along with the fuel, they keep burning. From this scene alone the argument against them is made, an intuitive argument: if these were gods, they would not have become the fuel of Hell. This is the true intuitive proof.

"Had these been gods, they would not have entered it." This scene which the Qur'an presents to them now in this world is presented in such a way as though it has already happened. They have practically reached the brink of Hell and have been cast into it, so now their condition in Hell is presented, in the manner of someone who is actually placed in such circumstances.

"And all will abide therein forever." (21:99) "For them therein is a roaring, and they will not hear therein." (21:100) "Now leave them here and let us see how the condition of the believers is. For them the decision has already been made in their favour. Success and salvation have already become their destination."

"The greatest terror will not grieve them, and the angels will receive them with welcome: 'This is your day, which you were promised.'"

This scene concludes with the scene of the end of this universe; this universe returns to that Day. In the frightening scene of that Day, just as the hearts of all people are in the grip of that terror, so the entire universe is also in the grip of that dread and alarm.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 21, verse 104:

"The Day We shall roll up the heavens as a scroll is rolled up for the writings" (21:103). "The day when We shall fold up the sky as the scroll of papers is folded up." The sky will be rolled up in the way a scroll of records is rolled up, one record over another. Now this scene ends, and this universe is folded up in the way our papers are folded up, and then there is a new world, a new universe, and a new cosmos.

"As We originated the first creation, so shall We bring it back again; a promise binding upon Us. Indeed, We shall certainly do it" (21:104). "Just as We began the first creation, so We shall repeat it. This is a promise upon Us, and this work is certainly to be done by Us."

After presenting this magnificent scene of the end of the universe, and of the re-creation of the world in the Hereafter, the discourse turns back again to this earth. The sunnah (way) of Allah is described: that the right of inheriting the sovereignty of this world belongs to My righteous servants, and this right has been given to them because they have proven themselves worthy of it by worshipping Allah in the world. There is a complete connection between these two scenes: the Hereafter belongs to the righteous servants, and the world also belongs to the righteous servants.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 21, verse 105:

ولقد………الصلحون (105)

The Zabur was a revealed scripture given to Dawud (peace be upon him). In this surah, the "Dhikr" (Reminder) would refer to the Torah, which was revealed before the Zabur. This is a description of the Book, meaning a part of the Book. The "part of the Book" in the sense of the Preserved Tablet (Lawh Mahfuz), which is a complete system and a complete reference, and within which all the laws connected with this universe are preserved. They are a part of it.

Nevertheless, the real issue under consideration is what is meant by it.

﴿And We had written in the Zabur, after the Reminder, that the earth would be inherited by My righteous servants.﴾ (21:105) What is inheritance? It means: what is God's law (sunnah) regarding the inheritance of this earth and supreme authority? That is, that authority here will be given to My righteous servants. Now the question is: who are the righteous servants?

Allah made Adam a khalifah (vicegerent) on the earth so that he would build and reform this earth, develop it, benefit from the treasures that Allah has deposited in it, put to use the natural forces within it, and carry this development to its ultimate limit, as far as Allah wills.

For this vicegerency on earth, Allah also gave humanity a methodology (manhaj), according to which humans are to work on the earth. The Prophet ﷺ made this methodology complete and detailed in his final message, and established laws and regulations for it. There is complete guarantee within these laws.

The aims of this system do not include only that humans, by putting to use the resources within the earth, emphasize material progress; rather, they also develop human intellect, human conscience and its spirit, so that the material and spiritual progress that humans are to achieve in this world reaches its end. It should not be that, while progressing materially in the world, they themselves, becoming mere animals, fall into decline. Material achievements should be touching the heavens while humanity is at the lowest depths of degradation (……).

When a person, performing the duties of the office of khilafah according to the Islamic system of life, is traveling the path of progress, the balance between material progress and spiritual progress sometimes gets disturbed too. Sometimes one side becomes heavy and sometimes the other, and balance does not remain. At times dictators, oppressors and rebellious people take possession of the sources of authority; sometimes utterly ignorant, boorish and adventurous people take over these positions; sometimes disbelievers and wicked people become dominant in these positions, who exploit the material and moral resources of the whole world. But these are only temporary experiences on the path. Allah's law is that inheritance of the positions on earth belongs to Allah's righteous servants, whose faith is complete and whose deeds are also correct. In their lives, faith and righteous deeds never become separated from one another.

Whenever, in the Ummah, faith and action have come together according to the Islamic standard, at any turning point in history, the earth has become the inheritance of the righteous servants. But when faith and action have been separated, that is, faith has been lost or action has been lost, this inheritance has slipped from their hands. Sometimes those who rely merely on material resources gain dominance. Those who are believers only in word and speech are left behind. Moreover, sometimes among the people of faith a formal faith remains, but it is not the true faith that moves a person to right action and worldly progress; in such a situation too, people who pursue only material progress take possession of the authority of the earth. This is because the people of faith are not fulfilling the requirements of that faith which Allah has prescribed for the people of faith, in the form of the Islamic system, for the lofty station of vicegerency on earth.

The workers of the Islamic movement have, at this time, only one duty: that they bring into their hearts the true meaning of faith. The true meaning of faith is righteous action. Then they must fulfill the requirements of vicegerency on earth. After that, Allah's sunnah does not delay even for a moment in its manifestation.

﴿Indeed, the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants.﴾ (21:105) Now, at the end, the strings of intellect and reason are struck by the same plectrum whose melodies were heard at the beginning of the surah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 21, verses 106–107:

"Indeed in this is a message for a people who worship." (21:106) That is, in the principles that the Quran has laid down for this entire universe and for human life, and in the natural outcomes it has described for people in this world (verse 105) and in the Hereafter, and in the principles of action and of recompense that it has established, there is great good news for these people, and only for those who are ready to act in accordance with Allah's guidance. Allah has used the word "ʿābidīn" (worshippers) for such people, because the one who worships and serves is always ready to accept every good and can benefit from it through reflection (tadabbur).

Allah the Exalted has sent Muhammad (ﷺ) as a guide for all of humanity, so that he might bring people to the path of Allah by seizing them and drawing them along. But it is only those who are prepared to be guided, who resolve to be guided, who actually attain guidance, although Allah's mercy is general for both believers and non-believers. The truth is that the system and the methodology (manhaj) that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought is, even in this world, a source of felicity for all of humanity. The message of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came in an era when humanity had reached maturity and adulthood. This message came in the form of an open book, and this book and this message present, for all future generations, a system of life in which there is no need for any change even in the future, because this system fulfils all the needs of human beings that may arise until the Day of Resurrection. This system is sent down by the Creator who knows human needs better than humans themselves, because He is Subtle and All-Aware.

Allah has laid down, within the Quran, principles that meet the new and ever-emerging needs of human life that will continue until the Day of Resurrection. He has left the branches and details to humanity itself, so that in the light of these principles they may enact laws for the developed life of humanity that will come until the Resurrection. In accordance with the circumstances of every age, they should make laws for partial matters through ijtihad (independent reasoning), provided that those laws do not conflict with the principles of the Quran, which are permanent.

The Quran gives a person complete freedom of intellect and thought; it raises a society in which people's minds are not locked. But the freedom of thought and action is within the boundary that the Islamic methodology (manhaj) has drawn, so that a person may grow in this worldly life, continue the process of progress, and carry it to the stage of perfection.

The experiences of humanity to date show that the system of life that Islam has established is ahead of all the systems of thought and action of humanity. It is capable of enabling humanity to progress continually in its light. This system always moves a person forward every moment; it neither freezes him nor pushes him backward, because it is a system whose very purpose is the vicegerency (khilafah fi al-ard) on earth. It develops this world, always moves forward, and its steps always go forward.

This system encourages the human drive for progress and fulfils the desire to move ahead. It places no restriction on the individual or collective capacities of a person. Nor does this system deprive a person of benefiting from the fruits of his struggle, nor does it impose a ban that he should not benefit from the pure things of life.

The position of this system is that it is balanced and harmonious. It does not crush the body so that the soul may flourish, nor does it suppress the soul so that the body may become fat. It fulfils the healthy physical needs and desires of a person, in such a way that they accord with individual and collective priorities. It does not permit the individual to let personal desires run so free and unbridled that the rights of society are affected, or that the interests of society are sacrificed for the interest of one person or of some persons.

In the duties and responsibilities that this system imposes on a person, it keeps in view that a person can bear them. They are within the limits of his capacity and strength, they are in his interest, and within him exists the ability to discharge these duties. Moreover, these duties are such that the individual is willing to perform them; indeed they are such that people not only accept them wholeheartedly but are even ready to give their lives for them, because these duties accord with their desires.

This is why the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) is a mercy for all humankind. The principles that this message brought were, at the beginning, regarded by people as strange and became a burden for them, because at the outset there was a great gap between Islamic principles and the spiritual and practical life of people. But after Islam came, humanity as a whole kept drawing closer, day by day, to the Islamic system. Humanity became familiar with the Islamic system, and then gradually adopted these principles in its own lands, though under other titles, not under the Islamic name.

This final message was meant to remove the linguistic, national and geographical boundaries that stood in the way of humanity, so that all people might become one in a single faith and a single system, a purely human system. At that time this was a strange and unusual call for people. In that era the nobles and great ones believed that they had not been created from the same clay from which the poor had been created. Yet fourteen hundred years ago Islam laid down human principles, and humanity is still moving slowly towards them today. Although in this period humanity has suffered great stumbles because it was deprived of the light of Islam, today it sees light in Islamic principles, and at least verbally it does speak of the human principles of Islam, though Europe and America are still caught up in the curses of national, linguistic and geographical divisions.

When Islam came, it gave all human beings equal standing before law and the court. At that time the condition of the world was that humanity had been divided into classes, and each class had its own separate law. Indeed, in the age of slavery and feudalism, the will of the master was the law. Therefore, in that era people found it strange that in Islam the slave and the master, the rich and the poor, are all under one law and one court. Yet the principle of equality before law and equality in access to judicial redress that Islam gave fourteen hundred years ago, humanity is still moving towards with heavy steps even today.

Apart from these matters, there are countless collective and social affairs in which the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) has proved a great mercy for people. You (ﷺ) have been sent as a mercy to the worlds, whether or not someone believed in you, because the system you brought affected all human beings, whether willingly or under compulsion, knowingly or unknowingly. The shade of this mercy still spreads; whoever wishes may come under it and find rest. In it are the pleasant breezes of the morning; its blessed tree gives deep shade, while the world around it is like a barren plain where a person wanders under the scorching heat of summer, burning.

The truth is that humanity today needs the mercy of Islam as it never has before. It is afflicted with painful anguish. It wanders and is distressed in the barren wilderness of materialism. It is caught in heaps of weapons and the law of the jungle in war, and materialism has dried up people's hearts. The souls of people are in terrible torment, and their hearts are troubled.

Therefore, after explaining that the mission of the Messenger (ﷺ) is a mercy for all humanity, the Messenger (ﷺ) is told to say to those who mock and deny: state the essence of the mercy of your mission.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 21, verse 108:

Translation: "Say: What is revealed to me is only that your God is one God. Will you then submit?"

In this message, the true element of mercy is this declaration (kalimah). The belief in Tawhid (the oneness of God) frees humanity from the superstitions of ignorance (jahiliyyah), the burden of idol-worship, and the burden of myths and customs. In this message, the whole of life is built upon this firm foundation of belief. Thus life comes into harmony with this entire universe. Humanity builds its life upon those natural laws which, on the one hand, operate throughout this universe and, on the other hand, operate in the Islamic system and the message of mercy. In the light of this system, every human being has the opportunity to walk with head held high upon this earth. If his head is to bow, let it bow only before the One God, the Almighty, the Compeller. Let it not bow before any tyrant of the world. This is the right way of life.

Fa-hal antum muslimun (21:108): "Will you then surrender and submit?"

This is the very question that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) puts to those deniers who mocked him.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 21, verse 109:

﴿Then if they turn away, say: "I have announced to you openly, and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far."﴾ (21:109)

"If they turn away, then say: I have announced to you openly." That is, I have laid my purpose before you in full. Now I and you are equal. "Idhan" (announcement) in fact refers to that declaration or ultimatum which is made when the period of peace is ending, and it is said to the other party that now there is war between the two sides. This surah is Meccan, and at that time fighting (qital) had not been made obligatory, so the meaning of the announcement here is that I have said whatever I had to say. Now it is for you, your own affairs and your own end. That is, this is the final announcement, and in future there will be no room for you to offer excuses or pleas. If they continue on their path knowingly and deliberately, the consequence (wabal) will also fall upon them, because they have knowledge.

﴿And I do not know whether it is near or far, that which you are promised.﴾ (21:109)

"I do not know whether that which you are promised is near or far." I have announced it to you openly, but it is not within my knowledge when the punishment you deserve will come, because it is one of the hidden, unseen knowledge of Allah. Only Allah knows about it. It is Allah alone who knows whether He seizes you in this world or in the Hereafter. He knows your secrets as well as your open words; nothing of yours is hidden from Him.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 21, verses 110–111:

"Indeed, He knows what is said openly and He knows what you conceal." (21:110) All your affairs lie open before Him. If He punishes you, He will punish you because He is aware of your outward and inward affairs alike; and if He delays the punishment, then some wisdom must still be in His view.

"And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and a provision for a time." (21:111) That is, why is your punishment being delayed? According to my knowledge, it is a further test for you. You are being given more respite, and after that you will be seized with great severity.

The fact that the time of the punishment is not fixed also contains an opportunity for them to take heed. When no time is specified, the possibility of the matter occurring is present at every moment, and a wise person may fear that it might suddenly come upon him. It is also possible that their hearts may emerge from the veils of heedlessness and they may realise that after this trial and respite, some calamity may befall them. If a calamity is certain to come but its time is not known, a thoughtful person is always apprehensive that the curtain may fall at any moment and the calamity appear before him.

Sometimes it also happens that a person is heedless of the matters that are waiting for him from behind the veil of the unseen, and the worldly provisions, comforts and pleasures deceive him further. A person forgets the matters that lie behind the veil; therefore, due to lack of knowledge, he becomes heedless. For this reason, Allah has deemed it necessary to warn people, and such heedless ones, so that they may become aware before the time arrives and make some arrangements for themselves.

The Messenger (ﷺ) delivered the trust, conveyed the message to the people, and proclaimed it openly. He also warned them of the sudden punishment of Allah. Now he is commanded to turn towards his Lord and to ask Allah to render a true judgment, and to requite these people for their plots, their denial and their mockery.

It is especially worth noting the mention of the attribute of mercy at the end. In this way the beginning and the end of the surah both come to be filled with the same theme, in a most impactful manner.
